entries.modern_form: PIE *keg-, *keng- / *kek-, *kenk- 'peg to hang things on, hook, handle; to be pointed' (Pokorny IEW 537-538; Walde-Pokorny I 382 f.); Mann's variant entries kag-/kaĝ- 'hook, claw; bend, angle, hook' (IEC 458)
entries.note: Pokorny 537-538 heads the entry exactly as Nourai names it: 'keg-, keng- und kek-, kenk- „Pflock zum Aufhängen, Haken, Henkel“; auch „spitz sein“; vgl. das ähnliche kak-, kank-; und kenk-, konk-'. Nourai's fifth name 'Kag' is not from Pokorny but from Mann, whose p.458 carries 'kag- (kagol-, kagil-) „hook, claw“' and 'kaĝ- (variant of type kag-) (1) „bend, angle, hook; bent“ ... Per. kaj (-ž) „bent“'; so the two cited references between them justify all five names and the gloss 'hook'. 'Kenk 2' is Nourai's own numbering of Pokorny's nasalised kenk-/konk- variant. The one substantive error in the chart is in node #1: the very form Pokorny prints under this root, čang, he labels 'Npers.' (New Persian), not Avestan; there is no Avestan *čanga- in Bartholomae's Altiranisches Wörterbuch. Everything else on the chart — čang > Arabic ṣanj, kaj/kaž, Germanic *hōka-/*hakkijan > hook/hack — is standard.

nodes.derivation: The form itself is real but the language label is wrong. Pokorny 537, the page Nourai cites, prints the word as 'Npers. čang „Klaue, Faust“ (*kengo-)' — i.e. as New Persian, the only Iranian witness he has for the root; the same word is Nourai's own node #2. Bartholomae's Altiranisches Wörterbuch has no *čanga-/cang at all (grep for 'cang/čang' returns nothing across BRT.txt), and no Avestan text attests such a word. Modern reconstruction goes only as far back as Proto-Iranian *čanga- 'claw', inferred from Middle Persian čang (Mo'in's footnote to Borhan s.v. چنگ gives 'pahlavi čang'), New Persian čang, and Old Armenian ճանկ (čank), which is itself an Iranian loan. So the arrow root → čang is right, but it should run to node #2 directly and be labelled Middle/New Persian, not Avestan.

nodes.derivation: NP چنگ čang 'claw, paw, hooked hand' continues MP čang (Mo'in's footnote to Borhan s.v. چنگ gives the Pahlavi form; MacKenzie's Pahlavi key has cang), from Proto-Iranian *čanga-, from PIE *keg-/*keng- 'peg, hook, claw' with the regular Indo-Iranian palatalisation of *k before a front vowel (*kenɡ- > *čanɡ-) and the equally regular Iranian retention of the nasal before the velar. The derivatives چنگال čangāl 'claw, fork' (čang + the instrument/collective suffix -āl) and چنگک čangak 'small hook' (+ diminutive -ak) are New Persian formations. Borhan-e Qate' p.665 glosses چنگ 'bent and curved; a hook in general; specifically the elephant-goad, also called کجک; the human paw and fingers; the claws of birds and beasts', i.e. exactly Nourai's 'hook, paw'. The third gloss 'harp' belongs to the same Middle Persian word čang 'harp' (Parthian šang); Wiktionary lists it as a separate etymology because the semantic bridge (the plucking hand, or the instrument's hooked frame) is not directly attested, but no source assigns it a different Indo-European root.
nodes.derivation_fa: «چنگ» از فارسی میانهٔ čang و آن از ایرانی آغازین *čanga- «چنگال» است که خود به ریشهٔ هندواروپایی آغازین *keg-/*keng- «میخ، قلاب، چنگال» می‌رسد؛ کاف هندواروپایی پیش از واکهٔ پیشین در هندوایرانی به چ دگرگون شده (کامی‌شدگی) و خیشوم پیش از گ بر جای مانده است. «چنگال» و «چنگک» ساخته‌های فارسی نو با پسوندهای ‌ال و ‌ک اند. برهان قاطع در صفحهٔ ۶۶۵ همین معانی «قلاب، پنجه، چنگال مرغان» را می‌آورد. معنای سوم یعنی ساز «چنگ» نیز همان واژهٔ فارسی میانه (پارتی šang) است؛ ویکی‌واژه آن را مدخل جداگانه آورده زیرا پل معنایی مستند نیست، ولی هیچ منبعی ریشهٔ دیگری برای آن نمی‌شناسد. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: Arabic صَنْج ṣanj is a Persian loan, but the two glosses Nourai gives have two different Persian sources. Asbaghi (PLA p.188) prints them as two entries on the same page: 'ṣang: „Kastagnetten“ ← pers. زنگ zang ← mp. sanj' and 'ṣangʲ: „persische Harfe“ ← pers. چنگ čang ← mp. čang; syr. ..., mand. singa'. So only the 'harp' sense is from čang: Persian č- was rendered by Arabic ṣ- (Arabic having no /č/, the emphatic sibilant being the regular substitute in early loans, cf. صولجان < چوگان), and the nasal + velar cluster gave -nj. The 'cymbal' sense, which is the ordinary modern meaning, Asbaghi derives from Persian zang 'bell, gong'. Lokotsch no.392 gives only the harp route ('Pers. cäng: „Harfe, Laute“, ar. ṣang „pers. Harfe, Leier“'), and Wiktionary agrees ('from Middle Persian čang „harp“ ... an obsolete term for harp; a cymbal'). The node is therefore right for 'harp', doubtful for 'cymbal'.
nodes.derivation_fa: «صنج» در عربی وام‌واژه‌ای فارسی است، اما دو معنایی که نورایی می‌آورد دو خاستگاه جدا دارند. اصبغی در «وام‌واژه‌های فارسی در عربی» صفحهٔ ۱۸۸ دو مدخل جداگانه دارد: صنج به معنی «سنج/قراقیز» از فارسی «زنگ»، و صنج به معنی «چنگ ایرانی» از فارسی «چنگ». در وام‌گیری، چ، که در عربی نیست، به صاد بدل شده است (همان‌گونه که چوگان > صولجان). لکوچ (شمارهٔ ۳۹۲) و ویکی‌واژه نیز تنها راه «چنگ» را می‌شناسند. پس ادعای نورایی برای معنای «harp» پذیرفتنی است و برای «cymbal» با احتیاط.

nodes.derivation: Persian صنج sanj/senj 'cymbal' is written with ص because it is the Arabic orthography coming back into Persian: Mo'in's dictionary tags the headword 'صنج: [معرّب سنج، قس. چنگ]', i.e. 'Arabicised form of سنج, compare چنگ'. The round trip Persian → Arabic → Persian that Nourai draws is therefore real and is exactly what Mo'in says. What is uncertain is the far end: if the Arabic word behind modern Persian صنج is Asbaghi's ṣanj 'castanets/cymbal', its Persian etymon was زنگ zang, and only the homonymous ṣanj 'harp' came from چنگ; the two fell together in Arabic and were re-exported as one word. Nourai's own cross-reference ('See root “Gěu 1” for another possible derivation') shows he was aware of the alternative, and modern scholarship (Asbaghi) prefers it for the 'cymbal' sense.
nodes.derivation_fa: «صنج» فارسی را با صاد می‌نویسند زیرا املای عربی آن دوباره وارد فارسی شده است؛ معین در فرهنگ خود می‌نویسد «صنج: [معرّب سنج، قس. چنگ]». پس رفت و برگشت فارسی ← عربی ← فارسی که نورایی ترسیم کرده واقعی است. آنچه جای تردید دارد سر دیگر زنجیره است: اگر صنج عربی به معنی سنج/قراقیز باشد، اصل آن پارسی «زنگ» است و تنها هم‌آوای آن به معنی جنگ/چنگ از «چنگ» آمده است. نورایی خود در یادداشت جعبه به ریشهٔ دیگری ارجاع داده و همین احتیاط درست است.

nodes.derivation: NP کج kaj / کژ kaž 'bent, crooked, awry' continues Middle Persian kaž (also gaz), from the same PIE *keg-/*kaɡ- family, with the o/zero-grade *kaɡ- of Mann's 'kaĝ- (variant of type kag-) „bend, angle, hook; bent“', where Mann's first witness is 'Per. kaj (-ž) „bent“'. The Iranian palatal outcome ž (later also j) of the palatalised velar is regular; the modern doublet کژ ~ کج is the ordinary NP alternation of ž/j. کژدم každom 'scorpion' is a transparent compound kaž 'crooked' + dom 'tail' ('crook-tail'); Wiktionary lists it under this etymology. Mo'in keeps the semantic bridge to the root explicit: he glosses کج both 'خمیده، ناراست، معوج' and 'قلاب' (a hook), so 'hook' and 'crooked' are one word in Persian lexicography too, exactly as the chart's root box implies. The Hāfez line quoted in the box ('وز خم ابروی توام هیچ گشایشی نشد...') uses خیال کج 'crooked/vain thought' in the figurative sense.
nodes.derivation_fa: «کج/کژ» از فارسی میانهٔ kaž (گونهٔ gaz) و آن از همان خانوادهٔ *keg-/*kaɡ- هندواروپایی «قلاب، خمیده» است؛ من در صفحهٔ ۴۵۸ مدخل kaĝ- «خمیده، کج» را دقیقاً با شاهد «Per. kaj (-ž)» می‌آورد. دگرگونی کاف کامی‌شده به ژ در ایرانی قاعده‌مند است و دوگانهٔ کژ ~ کج همان ابدال معمول ژ/ج در فارسی نو است. «کژدم» مرکّب کژ + دم یعنی «کج‌دم» است. معین خود در ذیل «کج» هم «خمیده، معوج» و هم «قلاب» را معنی کرده است؛ پس پیوند «قلاب» و «کج» همان است که در جعبهٔ ریشه آمده. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: Proto-Germanic *hōka- 'hook' is the lengthened-grade o-form of the root (*kāg- > Gmc *hōk- by Grimm's Law k > h and ɡ > k), beside the short-vowel *hakan- (ON haki, OE haca) and the geminated intensive *hakkijan 'to hack' (OE -haccian, MLG/MHG hacken), whose -kk- is the expressive gemination Pokorny notes ('mit intensiver Gemination: ags. haccian „hacken“'). Watkins' AHD appendix, Nourai's cited reference, sets out exactly these three Germanic stems under keg-.

nodes.derivation: OE hōc 'hook' > ME hok/hoke > NE hook, with the regular OE ō > ME ǫuː > NE /uː/ shortened to /ʊ/ before k. OE -haccian 'to cut to pieces' (attested in tō-haccian) > ME hakken > NE hack (verb), the noun being deverbal. Watkins lists HOOK and HACK as the English outcomes of keg-; Klein and Skeat agree, and Etymonline traces hook to OE hōc, PGmc *hōka-.

nodes.derivation: Young Avestan siiiāuua- (transliterated syāva-) 'black' = Sanskrit śyāvá- 'dark brown', from PIE *ḱih₃-wo- / *ḱyē-wo-, the extended colour stem of Pokorny's kie-. The compound Siiiāuuaršan- (syāva-aršan-) is the name of the Kayanid prince, Bartholomae analysing it 'Komp.: syava- + arsan-, eig. „der Rapphengste besitzt“' — literally 'owning black stallions', which is what the chart's '(with) “black male” animals' with the cross-reference to Eres 1 (aršan- 'male, stallion') means. syamaka- is the -ka- derivative, in Avestan the name of a mountain (Bartholomae col. 1631-32) but in Sanskrit an ordinary adjective 'dark-coloured'; the gloss 'owner of “black hair“' Nourai takes from Bartholomae's own footnote, which reports that the Bundahišn calls that mountain syāmō.gaonō 'with black hair'.

nodes.derivation: NP سیاه siyāh 'black' goes back through MP syā / siyāh (MacKenzie: 'syā [syʼ] | (P syʼw, N siyāh) black') to Old Iranian *syaHwa-/*syaHwaka-; Horn's no. 761 states the base form outright: 'Als Grundform von np. siyāh ist *syavaka- anzusetzen', the -aka- suffix giving the final -h after loss of intervocalic -k- and -a. سیاوش Siyāvaš is the regular NP reflex of Av. Siiiāuuaršan- (MP Siyāwaxš, with -rš- > -xš- and then NP -š), and سیامک Siyāmak of syamaka-. سیاه‌گوش siyāh-gūš 'caracal' is a NP compound siyāh + gūš 'ear' (< OP gauša-), i.e. 'black-ear', named for the animal's black ear-tufts. On the chart's own NOTE: it is correct — Turkish qara qulaq 'black ear' is a calque of exactly the same idea and is the etymon of English/French caracal (Klein s.v. caracal; Webster 'Turk. qara qulaq'), so Persian siyāh-gūš and Turkish qara-qulaq are parallel formations, not borrowings of one another.

Klein's entry gives the word and analyses it exactly as the chart does; Hobson-Jobson dates the English use to the 17th-19th centuries (A. Hamilton; Forbes, Oriental Memoirs i.277, 1813). It is a doublet of caracal, which reached English via French from the semantically identical Turkish qara qulaq.

nodes.derivation: The Shahnameh hero Sām, son of Nariman, father of Zāl and grandfather of Rostam, bears the family name that Avestan knows as ²sāma- (Bartholomae col. 1571), literally 'the black one'. Mo'in's own etymological footnote in his edition of Borhan-e Qate', on the very page Nourai cites, says so in as many words: 'در اوستا sāma (سیاه)، نام یک خانواده ایرانی است ... بارتولمه'. The name passes into MP and NP unchanged (the long ā is stable), and Mo'in adds that heroic tradition knows two Sāms, one the father of Aṭrat and one the descendant of Garšāsp and father of Zāl. He also warns that the homophonous سام 'Shem son of Noah' is a separate Hebrew word — a distinction the chart does not need to make.

nodes.derivation: Avestan saēna- 'a large bird of prey, probably the eagle' is built on Pokorny's variant root form kiei-, beside Sanskrit śyená- 'eagle, falcon' and śyenī- 'light-coloured' — i.e. the bird is named after its colour, which is why it sits under this root. Bartholomae col. 1548 gives '¹saēna- m. Name eines grossen Raubvogels, wohl des Adlers', citing Yt.14.41 mǝrǝgō saēnō. One correction of form: Avestan has the two-word phrase mǝrǝgō saēnō 'the bird saēna', not a compound *saēna-mǝrǝga- in that order; the univerbation is Middle Persian (sēn-murw), so Nourai's 'saēna-mereğa' is a normalisation of the Avestan phrase rather than an attested Avestan compound. The chart's cross-reference to root 'Mereğa' (Av. mǝrǝga- 'bird') is correct.

nodes.derivation: The two words in this box do not have the same fate. سیمرغ sīmorġ is confirmed: it continues MP sēn-murw (MacKenzie p.75: '²sēn murw [synmwlw | (N sīmurġ)] a fabulous bird'), which univerbates the Avestan phrase mǝrǝgō saēnō; Horn's no. 765, on the page Nourai cites, has 'sīmurġ „Greif, Adler; N. pr.“ ... aw. saenō mereγō- „Adler“; phlv. sīnmurō, sēn murūk (Yātkār-ī Zarērān p.64); ai. çyena- „Falke“'; the modern popular reading 'سی مرغ = thirty birds' is a folk etymology and Wiktionary labels it as such. شاهین šāhīn is not: the standard etymology is MP šāhēn 'royal, kingly' = شاه šāh (< OP xšāyaθiya-) + the adjectival suffix -ēn/-īn, i.e. 'the royal bird', which is also how Horn classifies it — not under sīmurġ (no.765) but under šāh (no.772, p.170: 'šāh „König, Herrscher“, šāhāne, šāhī, šāhīn „Falke“'), with the Armenian loan šāhēn as witness. Wiktionary agrees, citing Justi's Iranisches Namenbuch. Nourai's derivation from saēna- is not his invention — Mo'in's footnote in Borhan p.1237 offers it as a secondary possibility ('شاید هم شاهین همان ... saena (رک: سیمرغ) باشد که در اوستا نام عقاب است') — but even Mo'in gives شاه as the primary source, and the phonology favours it: Av. saēna- would give NP *sēn/sīn (as it does inside sīmurġ), never šāhīn with initial š- and long ā. Because one of the two words in the box is wrongly derived, the node takes the worse verdict.
nodes.derivation_fa: دو واژهٔ این جعبه سرنوشت یکسان ندارند. «سیمرغ» درست است: ادامهٔ فارسی میانهٔ sēn-murw است (مکنزی، صفحهٔ ۷۵) که خود یکی‌شدهٔ عبارت اوستایی mǝrǝgō saēnō است؛ هرن در شمارهٔ ۷۶۵ (صفحهٔ ۱۶۹) همین زنجیره را می‌آورد و خوانش عامیانهٔ «سی مرغ» ریشه‌شناسی عامیانه است. اما «شاهین» از saena- نیست: ریشه‌شناسی پذیرفته آن را از فارسی میانهٔ šāhēn «شاهانه»، یعنی شاه (از پارسی باستان xšāyaθiya-) + پسوند ‌ین می‌داند؛ هرن نیز آن را نه در مدخل سیمرغ بلکه در مدخل «شاه» (شمارهٔ ۷۷۲، صفحهٔ ۱۷۰) آورده است. معین در حاشیهٔ برهان قاطع (صفحهٔ ۱۲۳۷) احتمال saena را تنها با «شاید هم» می‌آورد و ریشهٔ اصلی را شاه می‌داند. از دید آوایی نیز saēna- در فارسی نو باید *سین می‌شد (چنان‌که در سیمرغ شده) نه شاهین.

nodes.derivation: Sogdian šʼw (Gharib's transcription sʼw, read šāw/šāu) 'black' is the eastern Iranian cognate of Avestan syāva-: Proto-Iranian *syāwa- gives Sogdian šāw by the regular Sogdian development of initial *sy- to š-, while the same cluster gives s- in Persian (siyāh) — the two branches diverge exactly here. Gharib herself glosses the entry with the Avestan etymon and the living cognates. The derivative šʼw-pʼmʼk 'blackish' (entry 9178) confirms the reading.

nodes.derivation: The root and the meaning are right, but the Germanic form is not the one the sources know. The Germanic word for 'colour, appearance' is neuter *hiwam (Gothic hiwi 'Schein, Aussehen', OE hīw/hēo, ON hý, Swedish hy), from PIE *ḱi-wo-; Watkins, the very reference the box cites, prints 'Suffixed zero-grade form *ḱi-wo- in Germanic *hiwam in Old English hīw, hēo, color, appearance, form: HUE'. A Germanic *hiwan- does exist, but it is a different word belonging to Pokorny's other root 1. kei- 'to lie, home': OE hīwan 'members of a household' (Watkins, ḱei-1: 'Germanic *hiwa- in Old English hīwan, members of a household: HIND'). Nourai's 'hiwan' therefore looks like *hiwam with -m misread or miscopied as -n, which happens to collide with the household word. I checked the printed page (pdf p.247 = book p.217, image saved as data/verification/sources/refs/ocr/BOOK/247.png): the book itself prints 'hiwan : color, hue', so the extraction is faithful and the slip is Nourai's own.

nodes.derivation: Latin cīmex, -icis 'bedbug' is derived by Pokorny (on the cited page) and by Klein from the reduced grade *kī-mo- of this colour root, the insect being named 'the dark-coloured one', with the -c- formant and consonantal declension of sene-x beside *seno-s; Prellwitz first proposed it (BB 30, 176) and Walde-Pokorny I 361 repeat it. Modern Latin etymology is more reserved: Ernout-Meillet, s.v. cimex, class it as 'mot populaire, même suffixe que dans culex, pulex' and conclude flatly 'sans étymologie, comme la plupart des mots de ce genre'; Etymonline likewise calls the Latin word 'of uncertain origin'. The chart's arrow is thus a respectable older view rather than a settled one, and the gloss 'black bug' is Nourai's rendering of Pokorny's parenthetical '„dunkelfarbig“', not a dictionary meaning.

nodes.derivation: Two different kinds of English word from the same Latin etymon. cimex is a learned zoological borrowing of the Latin nominative, the genus name of the bedbug (Cimex lectularius, Linnaeus 1758), taken directly into scientific and then general English. chinch 'bedbug' (and in America the chinch bug of wheat) came in about the 1620s through Spanish/Portuguese chinche, which continues the Latin accusative cīmicem by the ordinary Ibero-Romance treatment (-īc- > -č-, whence Sp. chinche; cf. the diminutive chinchilla). Klein and Etymonline give exactly this chain.
